ImageDescription.value: One sixth scale working model of an "Allen" two cylinder steam engine generating set on display in Bedford Museum. Built in 1957 by W H Allen apprentices and restored in 2006 by David Combes. It was made to run on compressed air but is currently being driven by an electric motor underneath it. When fully functional its output was 90 watts, but even now it still manages to light the bulbs on the left of the display. The original plaque describing it is here.

pages.title: File:Inner Range Light Lens.webm

ObjectName.value: Inner Range Light Lens

Categories.value: Duluth South Breakwater Inner Light|Files from external sources with reviewed licenses|Fourth order fresnel lenses|Uploaded with video2commons|Lighthouse fresnel lenses|Lighthouse Fresnel lenses on display|Videos of lighthouses

ImageDescription.value:
This video shows the original Duluth South Pier Inner Range Light fresnel lens in motion. It rotated around the light source and has flash panels that focused the light into distinct beams. This made the light appear to flash when viewed from a distance.

Originally, the mechanism that rotated the lens was a clockworks that worked very much like a large grandfather clock. Today it is rotated by an electric motor. The clockworks is still intact -- it is just no longer used.

This lens is on display in the Canal Park Marine Museum in Duluth, MN. It was removed from the lighthouse in 1995 due to deterioration of the lens. It was restored and placed on display inside the museum. The lighthouse now used a plastic fresnel lens that is rotated by an electric motor.

Credit.value: Inner Range Light Lens - Flickr

ObjectName.value: Florida Forests Flattened by Hurricane Michael, Now Fire Risk Looms - NBC Left Field

Categories.value: Media from YouTube|Videos from YouTube|License review needed (video)|Uploaded with video2commons|Videos of 2019 from the United States|Videos taken on 2019-06-07|Videos with text in English|Videos in American English|Videos of unidentified people of the United States|Videos by NBC News

ImageDescription.value:
What happens to a forestry community in the aftermath of a disaster? Hurricane Michael - a Category 5 storm - wiped out more than $1 billion worth of timber in the Florida Panhandle when it struck in October 2018, and nearly eight months later the community is still waiting for federal assistance to clean up and replant. The dead trees also mean that the panhandle is facing heightened wildfire risk, as a new hurricane season arrives.

Robby Roberts, a panhandle resident, was playing the long game when he planted his small plot of trees nearly 20 years ago, hoping it would provide him income in his later years. After Hurricane Michael ravaged his land, Roberts, a retiree, was able to sell half his timber for one ninth of the profit that he was expecting. The other half of what was to be his retirement plan now lies on the ground rotting. Roberts, like many other small land owners in the region, must now decide whether to reinvest in a crop that will take 20 years to see a return.
